newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Personality, not issues, focus of Chechen election.
newsitem.headline: Personality, not issues, focus of Chechen election.

text.p: Hussein is keen to vote in his region's first post-war election on January 27, but says his preferred presidential candidate is of secondary importance.

"Above all else I am voting for Chechnya's freedom and independence. Whoever becomes president we will all be under one command," Hussein, 54, told Reuters at a pre-election rally near the Chechen capital Grozny.
As a young man, he was deported along with most of his compatriots by Soviet dictator Josef Stalin, who said the Chechens were collaborating with Nazi Germany.
Hussein, who looks much older than his years, says he is just glad that Chechnya is at peace and free again.
The elections are a first step towards restoring order in Chechnya after a 21-month war between Russian troops and rebel fighters reduced much of the oil-rich region to rubble.

Moscow says it has now withdrawn its soldiers from Chechen territory in line with a peace deal signed last year. The rebel leaders have swopped their guns for microphones and their mountain hideouts for the campaign trail.
But only five of the 16 presidential candidates are considered serious contenders and they differ from each other more in personal style than in substance.

All back Chechen independence, which they regard as a fait accompli irrespective of Russia's steady opposition. The main candidates also favour a market economy and the Shariat, or Islamic legal code.
Candidates on the hustings begin and end their rallies with appeals to Allah and they generally refrain from speaking ill of their rivals.
"There is basically one camp with five candidates," said Tim Guldimann of the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) which is helping organise the elections.
Shamil Basayev, branded a terrorist by Moscow for his role in a spectacular raid on the southern Russian town of Budennovsk in June 1995, seems especially popular among the young.
The youthful, bearded Basayev has also attracted older voters with pledges to crack down on crime and restore order.
"Shamil is a good lad. He fought for us, we can rely on him," said pensioner Tamura Takayeva.

Aslan Maskhadov, former rebel chief-of-staff and probably Basayev's chief rival, takes a more pragmatic line on many issues, winning support of many tradespeople and of the few Russians still living in Chechnya.
Maskhadov, clean-shaven and soft-spoken, has indicated he is ready to work in a future government even if he is not elected president. Basayev is expected to return to private life if his bid fails.

Basayev has accused Maskhadov and acting president Zelimkhan Yandarbiyev -- also a key candidate in this month's poll -- of bringing supporters of Chechnya's former and widely despised pro-Moscow leader Doku Zavgayev back into government.
Both Maskhadov and Yandarbiyev have rejected the charges.
Guldimann played down talk that rebel leaders could start squabbling among themselves now that their common enemy -- the Russian army -- has left the scene.
"This is not Afghanistan," he told Reuters, referring to that country's descent into civil war after the Soviet military withdrawal. "I'm sure they can work together."
Guldimann said he was particularly encouraged by the fact that no party or group was boycotting the elections, which will also choose a 63-seat parliament.
The candidates know failure to cooperate would hamper sorely needed reconstruction in a region plagued by mass unemployment.
"We have our differences but there is not and will not be a split among us," another major presidential contender, former information minister Movladi Udugov, told Chechen television.
"The unity of the Chechen people will be preserved, regardless of who wins."
